young.html: René Descartes was a French thinker who wanted to be sure of what he knew. So he tried an experiment with his own mind. For a few days he would doubt everything he possibly could, and see if anything was left.

First he doubted his eyes and ears, because they sometimes fool us, like a straight stick that looks bent in water. Then he doubted that he was awake, because dreams can feel real. He even imagined a sneaky, powerful trickster who fooled him about everything, even about 2 + 3 = 5.

But then he found one thing he could not doubt. Even if he was being fooled, he had to exist to be fooled. Doubting is a kind of thinking, and someone has to be doing the thinking. “I am, I exist,” he wrote. That was his solid rock to build on.

young.cap: Step through the six meditations. Watch what gets knocked down and what is built back up.

young.html: The doubting game. Take turns saying something you believe (“It is Tuesday,” “My dog is in the yard,” “I have a nose”). The other players try to think of a way it could be wrong, even a silly one. Is there anything nobody can doubt? Talk about why “I am thinking right now” is so hard to doubt.

full.html: René Descartes (1596–1650) published the Meditations on First Philosophy in Latin in 1641, with a French version in 1647. Before printing it, he sent the manuscript to learned readers and printed their Objections with his Replies: from Thomas Hobbes, the theologian Antoine Arnauld, the philosopher Pierre Gassendi, Marin Mersenne's circle and others. His Discourse on the Method (its own rung) had sketched the same ideas for a wide audience in 1637; the Meditations work them out carefully, for scholars.

The book is written as six days of thinking by one person, in the first person, so that the reader can do the meditating too. Its stated aims are to show that God exists and that the mind is distinct from the body; along the way it tries to lay firm foundations for the sciences.

full.text: Meditation I: what can be doubted

full.html: Descartes resolves to doubt anything that is not completely certain, not because he thinks it is false but to find a foundation. The senses sometimes deceive; he may be dreaming; and he may have been made so that he goes wrong even about arithmetic. To keep himself from slipping back into old habits, he supposes something stronger:

full.text: I will suppose, then, not that Deity, who is sovereignly good and the fountain of truth, but that some malignant demon, who is at once exceedingly potent and deceitful, has employed all his artifice to deceive me…
full.author: René Descartes
full.ed: Descartes' Meditations and Selections from the Principles of Philosophy, Open Court

full.text: Meditation II: I am, I exist

full.html: Even if such a deceiver exists, he cannot make Descartes think he is something while he is nothing. So:

full.text: …so that it must, in fine, be maintained, all things being maturely and carefully considered, that this proposition (pronunciatum) I am, I exist, is necessarily true each time it is expressed by me, or conceived in my mind.
full.author: René Descartes
full.ed: Descartes' Meditations and Selections from the Principles of Philosophy, Open Court

full.html: But what is this “I”? Not, so far, a body, since bodies can still be doubted. It is a thinking thing:

full.text: But what, then, am I? A thinking thing, it has been said. But what is a thinking thing? It is a thing that doubts, understands, [conceives], affirms, denies, wills, refuses, that imagines also, and perceives.
full.author: René Descartes
full.ed: Descartes' Meditations and Selections from the Principles of Philosophy, Open Court

full.html: Then comes the piece of wax. Fresh from the honeycomb it has a color, a smell, a shape and a sound when tapped. Held near the fire, every one of these changes, yet we say it is the same wax. So what we know of the wax is grasped by the mind, not by the senses alone.

full.name: gb-doubt
full.cap: The six meditations. Choose a day to see what Descartes doubts and what he claims to have established.

items: III. I have the idea of an infinite, perfect being. Descartes argues that a finite mind could not produce such an idea by itself, so God must exist as its cause. A perfect God would not be a deceiver.
IV. Then why do I make mistakes? Because my will, which is unlimited, outruns my understanding, which is limited. If I affirm only what I see clearly and distinctly, I will not err.

V. The essence of material things is extension: length, breadth and depth, the subject of geometry. Descartes gives a second proof of God: existence belongs to the idea of a supremely perfect being as surely as three angles belong to a triangle.

VI. Mind and body are really distinct, since I can clearly understand one without the other; yet I am closely joined to my body, not just lodged in it the way a pilot sits in a ship. Since God is no deceiver, bodies exist, and my senses are a fair guide to what is useful and harmful, though not to the deep nature of things. Waking life hangs together in a way dreams do not.

full.html: The method of doubt is a tool, not a belief. Descartes doubts so that what survives can serve as a foundation. Ever since, philosophers have asked whether that foundation is enough to rebuild everything else.

full.title: The shape of the argument in Meditation II
full.q: Lay out the step from doubt to “I exist” as a short argument.
steps: Premise: I am doubting (or being deceived).
Premise: Doubting is a kind of thinking.
Premise: Whatever thinks must exist while it thinks.
Conclusion: I exist, at least while I think.
full.a: If I doubt, I think; if I think, I exist. So, while I think, I exist.

full.html: Thinking the famous Latin phrase “cogito, ergo sum” (“I think, therefore I am”) appears in the Meditations. Its best-known form is in the Latin Principles of Philosophy (1644); the French “je pense, donc je suis” is in the Discourse. The Meditations say “I am, I exist.”

deep.html: The printed Objections are part of the book. Hobbes doubted there was a separate thinking substance and suggested that thinking might be something a body does. Arnauld raised what is now called the Cartesian circle: Descartes uses clear and distinct ideas to prove God exists, then uses God to guarantee clear and distinct ideas. Gassendi pressed the empiricist case that ideas come from the senses. Later, Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia asked Descartes in letters (1643) how a mind that is not extended can move a body at all. Descartes answered each, and readers still judge for themselves how well.

Spinoza (next rung but one) rejected two separate substances and held that thought and extension are two attributes of one substance. Locke and Hume, in the next era, began from experience instead of certainty. Kant tried to explain why we cannot get outside our own way of knowing at all. In our own time, scientists and philosophers of mind still argue about how the mind relates to the brain.

items: Can you ever be completely certain you are not dreaming?
Is it possible to doubt everything, or does doubting itself depend on some beliefs?
Are you your body, your mind, or both together?

questions: Have your eyes or ears ever fooled you? How did you find out?
How do you know you are awake right now? Is that a good enough reason?
Why do you think Descartes printed his critics' objections in his own book?
The wax changes in every way we can see and smell, yet we call it the same wax. What makes something “the same thing” over time?
Is doubting something a good or bad habit? When is it each?
Descartes says mistakes come from jumping to conclusions. What helps you slow down before deciding?
